CM-1-2-1-3-4: Record exchange-executed futures and listed-options trades with contract, delivery month, quantity, price, account, clearing-broker, and allocation details; validate captured execution data against available execution and broker messages; and resolve trade-capture exceptions so the trading record reflects the executed cleared position.
CM-1-2-1-3-5: Record executed storage and throughput deals — facility, capacity, injection and withdrawal rights, fees, and period — so capacity positions, obligations, and costs are represented in the trading system from execution onward.
CM-1-2-1-3-6: Record executed purchases, sales, and transfers of program-specific environmental instruments — such as RINs, RECs, and emissions allowances — with program, vintage, quantity, price, and compliance-period detail, so instrument positions are accurate from execution onward.
CM-1-2-1-3-7: Record executed over-the-counter derivative trades — swaps, options, and other bilateral instruments, with underlying index, fixed and floating terms, notional quantity, tenor, and counterparty — flagging reportable transactions, so financial positions and obligations are accurate from execution onward.
CM-1-2-1-3-8: Record executed structured and non-standard transactions — multi-leg, embedded-optionality, tolling, prepay, and similar bespoke deals — decomposing them into capturable components so their positions, risks, and obligations are fully represented rather than approximated.
CM-1-2-1-3-9: Record executed transportation capacity deals — pipeline capacity, vessel charters, railcar commitments, and trucking capacity, with route or path, capacity, period, and rates — so transport positions, obligations, and costs are represented from execution onward.
CM-1-2-1-4: Develop, approve, and steward the trading strategies the front office runs — defining each strategy's objective, markets, instruments, and horizon, aligning it with approved authorities and risk limits, reviewing performance, and adjusting or retiring strategies as conditions change.
CM-1-2-2-1-1: Assess a counterparty's creditworthiness — at onboarding, on a periodic cycle, and on trigger events — analyzing financial statements, ratings, ownership and support structures, payment behavior, and qualitative factors, and assigning or updating the internal credit assessment that limits and monitoring run on.
CM-1-2-2-1-2: Establish, maintain, publish, and adjust credit limits for trading counterparties and counterparty groups — based on approved credit assessments, risk appetite, exposure methodology, and credit-support arrangements — administer documented temporary-excess and exception decisions under delegated authority, and reduce, suspend, or withdraw limits when deterioration or policy triggers require it.
CM-1-2-2-1-3: Administer contractual credit support both held and posted — cash collateral, securities, letters of credit, guarantees, and other eligible security, with their haircuts, thresholds, independent amounts, and substitutions — calling, receiving, returning, valuing, and reconciling credit support under the applicable arrangements, so credit exposure is secured to the extent the agreements require.
CM-1-2-2-1-4: Calculate current and, where required by approved methodology, potential future credit exposure for each counterparty and group — aggregating trading positions, mark-to-market values, delivered-but-unpaid and other settlement-cycle exposures, and applicable netting, collateral, and credit-support effects — so limits, monitoring, and credit support run on a defensible exposure number.
CM-1-2-2-1-5: Administer margin obligations for cleared and other applicable margined positions — receiving, validating, forecasting, and issuing or responding to margin calls as applicable, reconciling margin balances against CCP, exchange, broker, and counterparty statements, and escalating failed or disputed calls — so margin obligations are met and margin held matches what positions require.
CM-1-2-2-1-6: Analyze credit risk at portfolio level — concentrations, stress and scenario impacts, default-likelihood signals, and correlation effects such as wrong-way exposure — so appetite, limits, and mitigation decisions rest on more than single-counterparty views.
CM-1-2-2-1-7: Continuously watch counterparty credit — exposures against limits, breach detection and aging, and early-warning signals from ratings, news, payment behavior, and market indicators — escalating breaches and deterioration per policy and triggering reassessment where warranted.
CM-1-2-2-1-8: Produce governed internal credit-risk reports — exposures, limit utilization, breaches, credit-support and margin positions, and concentrations, at agreed cadences and levels for management and committees — and provide controlled inputs to applicable external or regulatory reporting through their accountable owners, so the credit risk picture is current, consistent, and decision-ready.
CM-1-2-2-2-1: Produce and dispatch outgoing trade confirmations from captured deal records — using the templates and terms of the governing agreement — and match incoming counterparty confirmations or equivalent contractual acknowledgements against the captured deal record, using the applicable product, agreement, and confirmation standards, chasing unconfirmed trades within applicable timeliness requirements.
CM-1-2-2-2-2: Maintain the confirmation documentation basis — approved templates and standard wording aligned to governing agreements, the archive of dispatched and matched confirmations, and the evidence trail that shows what was agreed and when — so confirmations are consistent, current, and provable.
CM-1-2-2-2-3: Coordinate the confirmation-side processing of agreed post-execution changes to a trade — including amendments, allocations, partial terminations, and early terminations — by validating counterparty agreement, initiating or validating the required controlled trade-record update, re-confirming revised terms, and triggering applicable lifecycle reporting.
CM-1-2-2-2-4: Report confirmation and lifecycle events for reportable transactions under an applicable trade-reporting regime — submitting required continuation data for amendments, terminations, and other post-execution events to the designated registered swap data repository within applicable deadlines, where the organization holds reporting responsibility — correcting errors and retaining reporting evidence.
CM-1-2-2-2-5: Resolve confirmation mismatches and disputes — logging discrepancies between the capture record and the counterparty's confirmation, investigating against execution evidence, agreeing the correct terms with the counterparty, and driving the resolution into the records and any required re-reporting.
CM-1-2-2-3-1: Establish and maintain the governed trading-book and portfolio hierarchy used for risk aggregation, valuation, position control, and P&L reporting — defining risk-reporting book attributes, responsible owners, aggregation relationships, and effective-dated changes — and keep trading, risk, and reporting systems aligned to it.
CM-1-2-2-3-10: Monitor adherence to the organization's own market-risk policies and control framework — mandate and delegation-of-authority adherence, control-cycle completion, exception-procedure use, and policy-required documentation — surfacing violations and control gaps to the accountable owners.
CM-1-2-2-3-11: Define, maintain, and run the market-risk scenario and stress set — historical and hypothetical market shocks, commodity and basis stresses, and event scenarios — quantifying their P&L and risk impacts so the organization knows what adverse markets would do to the book before they happen.
CM-1-2-2-3-12: Analyze market risk beyond the standard measures — backtesting the measures against outcomes, analyzing model behavior and measure limitations, investigating risk concentrations and emerging exposures, and developing analytical improvements — recommending changes to methodologies, limits, and controls.
CM-1-2-2-3-13: Produce governed internal market-risk reports — measures, limit utilization, breaches, scenario results, positions, and P&L, at agreed cadences for management and committees — and provide controlled inputs to applicable external or regulatory reporting through their accountable owners.
CM-1-2-2-3-14: Source, construct, validate, and publish the volatility and correlation parameters that option valuation and risk measurement depend on — by commodity, location, and tenor per approved methodology — so valuations and measures rest on governed market parameters, not ad hoc inputs.
CM-1-2-2-3-15: Produce and control the official valuations of the trading book — marking positions to market or, where approved, to model per approved methodology from the official curves and parameters, applying approved valuation adjustments, investigating exceptions, and publishing the valuations that P&L, risk, exposure, and reconciliation run on.
CM-1-2-2-3-2: Establish and maintain the trading delegation of authority — who may trade what products, instruments, tenors, and sizes, and which approvals are required beyond each authority — keeping it current with roles, strategies, and governance decisions so every trade's authorization has a defined basis.
CM-1-2-2-3-3: Construct and maintain the forward price curves the organization values and measures risk with — sourcing market data, building and validating curves by commodity, location, and tenor per approved methodology, and publishing the official curve set on the control calendar.
CM-1-2-2-3-4: Coordinate and evidence the daily trading-risk control cycle — performing or obtaining capture-completeness checks, freezing the official market-data set, running or obtaining valuation, position, P&L, and risk-measure outputs, investigating material exceptions, and obtaining the designated control approvals for the daily controlled result.
CM-1-2-2-3-5: Coordinate and evidence the month-end trading-risk control cycle — reconciling and reviewing the month's daily controlled results, producing month-end economic valuation, position, P&L, and risk outputs, resolving or formally carrying forward approved exceptions — and provide the controlled economic inputs required by Accounting's reconciliation and close processes.
CM-1-2-2-3-6: Establish, maintain, publish, and adjust market-risk limits — by book, strategy, commodity, tenor, and measure — derived from approved risk appetite; administer documented temporary-excess and exception decisions under delegated authority; and tighten or suspend limits when conditions or policy triggers require it.
CM-1-2-2-3-7: Compute the organization's market-risk measures — value-at-risk, sensitivities, position and tenor exposures, and the other measures the approved framework requires — from validated positions, curves, and volatilities, publishing them on the control calendar so limits, monitoring, and reporting run on one measured picture.
CM-1-2-2-3-8: Continuously watch market risk against limits — detecting breaches and near-breaches, escalating them per policy, tracking them to resolution, and watching concentration and regime signals — so no excursion goes unseen or unescalated.
CM-1-2-2-3-9: Produce and analyze the official, controlled position and realized and unrealized P&L picture — explaining daily P&L by its drivers (price, position, new deals, amendments, and other effects), investigating unexplained amounts, and delivering the validated P&L that management, risk, and the accounting reconciliation consume.
CM-1-2-3-1-1: Actualize pipeline movements of crude, feedstocks, and products — recording actual receipt and delivery volumes, qualities, and dates from pipeline meter tickets, carrier statements, and shipper reports, applying pipeline loss allowance, quality-bank, proration, or other carrier and tariff adjustments where applicable, and reconciling actuals against nominated and scheduled volumes — so pipeline transactions settle on verified actuals.
CM-1-2-3-1-2: Actualize truck movements of crude, feedstocks, and products — recording actual loaded and delivered volumes, qualities, and dates from bills of lading, terminal lifting records, and truck tickets, recorded on the contractually applicable measurement and temperature/volume basis — so truck transactions settle on verified actuals.
CM-1-2-3-1-3: Actualize railcar movements of crude, feedstocks, and products — recording actual loaded and received quantities, weights, qualities, and dates from railcar shipping documents, scale weights, and gauging records on the contractually applicable basis — so rail transactions settle on verified actuals.
CM-1-2-3-1-4: Actualize marine movements by vessel and barge — recording actual loaded and outturn quantities, qualities, and dates from bills of lading, independent inspection reports, and ship and shore figures per marine measurement practice, and identifying apparent voyage gains, losses, and quantity differences according to the contractual measurement basis — so marine transactions settle on verified actuals.
CM-1-2-3-1-5: Actualize terminal and storage transactions — recording transaction-level receipt, delivery, throughput, and contractually relevant storage-balance actuals for the associated deal or capacity arrangement from terminal operator statements, tank gauging records, and throughput reports, and recording verified throughput, storage, blending, and handling charge determinants and applicable contractual bases — so terminal and storage transactions settle on verified actuals.
CM-1-2-3-1-6: Actualize crude and condensate lease purchases — recording actual volumes, gravities, and qualities from run tickets and LACT meter records taken at lease-tank custody transfer, applying the contractual gravity, quality, and deduction adjustments and division-of-interest references — so first-purchase transactions settle on verified actuals.
CM-1-2-3-1-7: Update environmental-attribute and renewable-instrument trading records from authoritative registry lifecycle events — including issuance or generation, separation where applicable, transfer, acquisition, sale, retirement, and cancellation — and reconcile internal instrument positions to the applicable registry or regulatory system of record.
CM-1-2-3-1-8: Manage disputes over what was physically delivered, received, measured, or performed — logging and classifying quantity, quality, and measurement discrepancies, investigating against custody-transfer evidence and independent inspection, coordinating investigation, evidence exchange, and agreement or adjudication of corrected actuals with the relevant external parties under the governing agreement and applicable measurement hierarchy, and closing disputes through corrected actualized records.
CM-1-2-4-1-1: Settle physical crude oil and condensate purchases and sales — applying contractual pricing, including provisional pricing, deferred pricing, or subsequent price determination where the contract provides, and contractually defined quality adjustments to actualized volumes, issuing and validating invoices, netting where agreements allow, and submitting authorized payment and receipt instructions — so crude transactions complete financially on verified actuals.
CM-1-2-4-1-10: Settle natural gas purchases, sales, transportation, and storage — applying index and contract pricing to scheduled and flowing-gas quantities, validating pipeline and counterparty invoices per the applicable business-practice standards, settling imbalances and cash-outs per tariff and contract, and submitting authorized payment and receipt instructions — so gas transactions complete financially on verified quantities.
CM-1-2-4-1-11: Settle bilateral financial over-the-counter derivatives — determining settlement amounts from contractual fixings and floating-price observations per the confirmed terms, exchanging and validating settlement calculations with counterparties, netting payments under the governing master agreements, and submitting authorized payment and receipt instructions — so financial trades complete per their documented terms.
CM-1-2-4-1-12: Settle pipeline transportation charges with carriers — validating pipeline invoices for tariff transportation, fuel, loss allowance, and related charges against actualized pipeline movements and verified tariff determinants, resolving variances, and submitting authorized payment instructions — so pipeline services complete financially on verified movement actuals.
CM-1-2-4-1-13: Settle rail transportation charges with railroads and rail service providers — validating freight and accessorial invoices against actualized rail movements and verified charge determinants, applying contracted and tariff rates, resolving variances, and submitting authorized payment instructions — so rail services complete financially on verified movement actuals.
CM-1-2-4-1-14: Settle terminal and storage service charges — validating operator invoices for throughput, storage, blending, handling, and ancillary services against actualized terminal transactions and verified charge determinants and contractual bases, resolving variances, and submitting authorized payment instructions — so terminal and storage services complete financially on verified actuals.
CM-1-2-4-1-15: Settle bilateral power transactions outside ISO markets — applying contract and index pricing to scheduled and delivered quantities, validating counterparty invoices and settlement data, netting where agreements provide, and submitting authorized payment and receipt instructions — so bilateral power transactions complete financially on verified quantities.
CM-1-2-4-1-16: Settle broker and clearing-member account activity — reconciling broker statements against internal trade, position, and margin records, validating commissions, fees, and charges, preparing, submitting, tracking, and reconciling authorized broker-facing payment or collateral-transfer instructions, including margin transfers, through the designated Treasury, banking, or payment-operations process, and resolving statement discrepancies — so broker accounts remain accurate, funded, and evidenced.
CM-1-2-4-1-17: Manage disputes over what is owed, invoiced, received, paid, netted, or applied — logging and classifying settlement discrepancies, investigating against actualized records, contractual terms, and settlement calculations, coordinating resolution with counterparties, carriers, brokers, and operators under the governing agreements, escalating aging or material disputes, and closing them through corrected settlements and evidenced adjustments.
CM-1-2-4-1-18: Settle purchases and sales of refinery intermediates and blend components — applying contractual and index-based pricing to actualized volumes and qualities, generating and validating invoices, netting where agreements provide, and submitting authorized payment and receipt instructions — so intermediate transactions complete financially on verified actuals.
CM-1-2-4-1-19: Settle purchases and sales of other commodities traded by the organization — such as NGLs, petrochemicals, sulfur, petroleum coke, and other by-products or ancillary commodities — applying contractual pricing to actualized quantities, generating and validating invoices, and submitting authorized payment and receipt instructions on the same settlement discipline as the named commodity processes.
CM-1-2-4-1-2: Settle physical refined product purchases and sales — applying contractual and index-based pricing to actualized volumes on the contractual measurement basis, generating and validating invoices, netting where agreements provide, and submitting authorized payment and receipt instructions — so product transactions complete financially on verified actuals.
CM-1-2-4-1-3: Settle exchange-traded and cleared transactions — validating and allocating daily settlement variation and final settlement amounts to trades and positions against exchange and clearinghouse values, settling expiries, exercises, and deliveries per contract specifications, and reconciling trade-level settlement outcomes — so cleared positions complete financially per exchange rules.
CM-1-2-4-1-4: Settle truck transportation charges with carriers — validating freight invoices against actualized movements and verified freight-charge determinants, applying contracted rates and accessorials, resolving invoice variances, and submitting authorized payment instructions — so trucking services complete financially on verified movement actuals.
CM-1-2-4-1-5: Settle marine transportation charges — validating freight, charter hire, and voyage-related invoices against actualized voyages and verified freight, laytime, and voyage-cost determinants, applying charter party and freight-agreement terms, resolving variances, and submitting authorized payment instructions — so marine services complete financially on verified voyage actuals.
CM-1-2-4-1-6: Settle crude and condensate first-purchase transactions — calculating amounts due from actualized lease runs under contractual pricing, gravity and quality adjustments, and deductions, producing settlement statements consistent with the division-of-interest references, and submitting authorized payment instructions — so lease purchases complete financially on verified run actuals.
CM-1-2-4-1-7: Settle transactions with independent system operators, regional transmission organizations, and power pools — validating ISO settlement statements across the day-ahead and real-time settlement cycles and their subsequent true-up versions, performing independent shadow-settlement checks, disputing discrepancies within ISO timelines, and submitting authorized payment and receipt instructions — so ISO-cleared activity completes financially per market rules.
CM-1-2-4-1-8: Settle environmental and renewable instrument transactions — RINs, allowances, RECs, and similar program instruments — calculating amounts due from actualized registry transfers and contractual pricing, generating and validating invoices, and submitting authorized payment instructions against confirmed instrument delivery — so instrument trades complete financially on verified registry actuals.
CM-1-2-4-1-9: Manage the controlled working and evidentiary document set used by trading settlement — generating, receiving, validating, distributing, and retaining settlement statements, payment instructions, supporting actualization evidence, and applicable invoices — so every settlement is executed and evidenced from controlled, complete documents.
CM-1-2-4-2-1: Assess, document, and apply the accounting treatment of trading transactions under approved enterprise policy — derivative versus normal purchase/normal sale scope, own-use, lease, storage, and exchange treatments, and gross-versus-net presentation — obtaining Finance/controller approval or escalation for material, new, complex, or policy-sensitive conclusions, so transactions are recorded under the correct, evidenced treatment.
CM-1-2-4-2-10: Calculate, post, and true up accruals for trading activity — un-invoiced delivered or received volumes, expected fees and charges, and estimated prices pending final determination — per the enterprise accrual methodology, so each period's books are complete for activity not yet settled.
CM-1-2-4-2-11: Execute transaction- and commodity-tax accounting for supply and trading activity by applying approved tax rules and tax-determination data to transactions, recording tax amounts, maintaining required transaction-level evidence, and preparing controlled tax-accounting and filing-support outputs for the accountable enterprise Tax function.
CM-1-2-4-2-12: Develop, maintain, version, and communicate trading-specific accounting procedures, close instructions, and implementation guidance that operationalize Finance-owned enterprise accounting policy for supply and trading activity.
CM-1-2-4-2-2: Maintain the financial accounting of production and inventory for supply and trading activity — recording and reconciling financial inventory balances and cost-of-sales effects under the enterprise-approved inventory valuation methodology, from verified operational balances — so the financial books carry a complete, correctly valued representation of physical activity.
CM-1-2-4-2-3: Execute royalty and interest disbursements arising from first-purchase and marketing arrangements — calculating owner-level distributions from settled lease transactions and division-of-interest references, managing suspense and unclaimed amounts per the applicable requirements, and submitting authorized disbursement instructions — so interest owners are paid correctly and on time.
CM-1-2-4-2-4: Record trading receivables, payables, and actuals in the accounting records — recording authorized settlement outcomes and validated invoices in AR/AP, posting actualized transaction values, monitoring open items and aging, and keeping the payables and receivables position complete and current — so the financial position reflects settled and actualized activity.
CM-1-2-4-2-5: Maintain the trading sub-ledger as the complete transactional accounting record — ensuring every captured, actualized, and settled transaction posts correctly under its determined treatment, reconciling the sub-ledger to the general ledger, and enforcing period cut-off — so the general ledger can rely on a complete, reconciled trading record.
CM-1-2-4-2-6: Reconcile the economic profit and loss produced by the trading risk processes to the profit and loss recorded in the accounting books — identifying, quantifying, explaining, and evidencing expected and unexpected differences by cause — so management, risk, and financial views of trading results are provably consistent.
CM-1-2-4-2-7: Prepare and control the financial documentation and internal financial reporting for supply and trading activity — management reporting on financial results, accounting workpapers and reconciliation evidence, and controlled inputs to external financial reporting through the accountable owners — so financial information about trading is complete, evidenced, and consistently produced.
CM-1-2-4-2-8: Administer the financial system structures used by trading accounting — chart-of-accounts mapping, ledger and book structures, posting rules and business interface configuration from trading systems to the general ledger, and accounting master data — so postings land correctly, completely, and controllably in the financial records.
CM-1-2-4-2-9: Apply cash receipts to open trading receivables — matching bank-reported receipts against invoices, settlement statements, and netting arrangements, investigating and coordinating resolution of unapplied, unidentified, short, and over payments, and evidencing application — so the receivables position is accurate and cash is accounted for daily.
CM-1-2-4-3-1: Develop and maintain the trading compliance program's policies and procedures — market-conduct rules, information barriers, personal-account dealing, communications and conflicts requirements, regulatory-change management, and compliance monitoring and escalation procedures — within the enterprise compliance and legal governance framework, so trading activity operates under current, communicated compliance requirements.
CM-1-2-4-3-2: Monitor supply and trading activity for compliance with external law, regulation, and market rules — market-conduct and anti-manipulation surveillance, position-limit monitoring, exchange and market-rule adherence, licensing and registration status, and completion of regulatory reporting obligations by their owners — surfacing potential violations for assessment and escalation.
CM-1-2-4-3-3: Monitor adherence to the organization's internal trading compliance policies — conduct rules, information barriers, personal-account dealing, gifts and entertainment, communications requirements, and required compliance training — surfacing violations and adverse patterns for assessment and escalation.
CM-1-2-4-3-4: Monitor the operation of internally implemented controls that support the organization's external trading obligations — verifying that required deal approvals are evidenced, regulatory reporting controls are complete and functioning, surveillance and recordkeeping controls operate as designed, and audit evidence exists — surfacing control failures and gaps to the accountable owners.
CM-1-2-4-3-5: Monitor and assure compliance with transaction- and commodity-tax obligations affecting supply and trading activity by reviewing evidence of registration, licensing, exemption-certificate, filing-calendar, and tax-determination-control compliance; coordinating relevant tax-authority notices and examinations with the enterprise Tax function; and escalating material gaps.
CM-1-2-4-3-6: Coordinate the trading organization's Renewable Fuel Standard reporting obligations — assembling and quality-assuring RIN transaction, position, and renewable-volume-obligation data from the trading systems and registries, reconciling it to EMTS, and preparing controlled reporting inputs and supporting evidence for the accountable filer — so RFS reports attributable to trading activity are complete, accurate, and evidenced.
CM-1-2-4-3-7: Manage compliance exceptions through their lifecycle — logging and classifying identified violations, control failures, and approved deviations, assessing severity and regulatory implications, coordinating waiver, remediation-plan, and closure approvals under the documented compliance delegation, tracking remediation to closure, and evidencing the record — so every compliance gap is visibly owned, decided, and closed.
CM-1-2-4-4-1: Screen completed voyages and terminal operations for potential demurrage, despatch, and detention entitlements and exposures — comparing used against allowed laytime from actualized notices, statements of fact, and timesheets under the governing terms, computing preliminary claim values in both directions, and identifying the contractual deadlines and evidence needed to preserve or defend each claim — so every potential claim is identified before rights lapse.
CM-1-2-4-4-2: Build outbound demurrage, despatch, and detention claims — performing the definitive laytime calculation under the governing terms, assembling the supporting evidence (notices of readiness, statements of fact, timesheets, port and terminal logs), verifying contractual notice, documentation, and time-limit requirements are met, obtaining the designated internal review, and issuing the claim to the responsible party — so outbound claims are complete, timely, and defensible.
CM-1-2-4-4-3: Register inbound demurrage, despatch, and detention claims — logging received claims, acknowledging where the governing terms require, recording receipt-stage time-limit and documentation observations, and routing claims to assessment — so inbound claims enter a controlled process with their receipt-stage observations captured.
CM-1-2-4-4-4: Assess the merit and quantum of inbound claims — recalculating laytime independently from the organization's own actualized records under the governing terms, applying contractual exceptions, interruptions, allocation provisions, notices, and responsibility rules as the governing agreement provides, and determining an evidenced accept, counter, or reject position — so inbound claims are paid only to the extent actually owed.
CM-1-2-4-4-5: Pursue issued outbound claims to resolution — presenting the claim and its evidence, responding to counterarguments and counter-calculations, negotiating commercial resolution within delegated claim-settlement authority, obtaining additional approval where a proposed compromise, waiver, credit, set-off, or write-down exceeds that authority, and agreeing resolution or escalating unresolved claims — so outbound entitlements convert to agreed, collectible amounts.
CM-1-2-4-4-6: Resolve inbound claims from the assessed position — communicating the assessed position with its evidence, negotiating, accepting, partially accepting, countering, or rejecting the claim within delegated authority, routing concessions, waivers, or formal settlement agreements through the required approval path, and agreeing resolution or escalating unresolved claims — so inbound exposure closes at the evidenced amount, not the claimed one.
CM-1-2-4-4-7: Invoice agreed outbound claims — issuing the claim invoice and settlement statement for the negotiated amount with its supporting calculation, submitting the receivable into the designated finance processes, tracking expected receipt, and obtaining confirmation from Accounting that the receivable is booked and cash applied — so agreed entitlements are collected and evidenced.
CM-1-2-4-4-8: Process invoices for agreed inbound claims — validating the received invoice against the negotiated resolution and its evidence, preparing and submitting a payment request supported by the agreed resolution and required approvals to the designated Accounts Payable/Treasury process, and evidencing closure — so the organization pays exactly what was agreed, once, with a complete trail.
CM-1-2-5-1-1: Steward the crude and feedstock quality data used in evaluation, planning, and trading — maintaining current, validated assays and quality records, tracking assay age and representativeness, incorporating new laboratory and cargo data under controlled update procedures, and distributing consistent quality data to the consuming models and processes.
CM-1-2-5-1-2: Review whether the feedstock data, yield representations, operating constraints, capacities, market assumptions, and other decision inputs used by feedstock-evaluation and planning models remain current, complete, internally consistent, and representative of the refinery and market conditions; document findings and escalate required corrections to accountable data and model owners.
CM-1-2-5-1-3: Develop the recommended term feedstock procurement slate — the portfolio of crudes and feedstocks proposed for supply under agreements with multi-period or continuing commercial commitments, screened for refinery quality compatibility and evaluated for sustained economic attractiveness — so term procurement and the feedstock recommendation rest on a quality-assured base-load supply plan.
CM-1-2-5-1-4: Develop the recommended spot feedstock procurement slate — the quality-screened spot supply candidates that address residual demand, supply disruption, quality constraints, timing needs, or economic opportunities after considering committed term supply, ranked by current economic attractiveness and availability — so spot procurement decisions start from a vetted, refinery-compatible option set.
CM-1-2-5-2-1: Coordinate feedstock supply requirements with the trading processes — translating demand, slate recommendations, and schedule imbalances into requested purchases, sales, or exchanges with their grade, quality, quantity, timing, and delivery requirements, evaluating proposed trades for plan and schedule fit, and incorporating agreed volumes back into the supply plan.
CM-1-2-5-2-2: Develop the projected feedstock requirement — quantity, grade, quality, and timing — from the refinery production plan and current inventory and supply positions, maintaining it as plans and positions change, so procurement, slate development, and trading coordination work from one validated demand signal.
CM-1-2-5-2-3: Recommend the economically attractive feedstock slate and run rate to Refinery Planning — combining the demand signal, procurement slates, market prices, and supply economics into a trading-side recommendation that feeds the binding plan without setting it — so the refinery plan is informed by the best current supply-market view.
CM-1-2-5-3-1: Coordinate and monitor the commercial and logistical arrangements required to move agreed feedstock volumes under available carrier contracts, capacity rights, nominations, fixtures, and transport agreements — selecting modes and routings, tracking movement status, and resolving in-transit issues with carriers and operators — so every purchased cargo has a managed path to the refinery.
CM-1-2-5-3-2: Schedule feedstock deliveries into agreed refinery receipt windows by sequencing confirmed movements against available berth, pipeline-receipt, tankage, quality-segregation, and refinery-receipt constraints, coordinating and confirming proposed receipt windows with the relevant refinery and terminal scheduling and operations owners, and maintaining the delivery schedule as movements and refinery conditions change.
CM-1-2-5-3-3: Plan individual feedstock arrivals — coordinating laycans, arrival timing, and berth and discharge sequencing with the terminal and refinery, recommending or coordinating proposed tank destinations with refinery/terminal operations subject to their operational authority, and adjusting the arrival plan as vessels, pipelines, and refinery conditions develop — so each arrival is prepared for timely, safe, and quality-compatible receipt, subject to operational conditions and the governing agreements.
CM-1-2-5-4-1: Assess the price, supply-availability, disruption, quality, concentration, and working-capital risk associated with feedstock inventory positions; recommend inventory, supply, operational, and hedging mitigations to accountable owners; and submit approved hedging requirements to the authorized trading process so risk is visible, understood, and managed within approved appetite.
CM-1-2-5-4-2: Monitor and control actual and projected crude and feedstock inventory positions — identifying operating-limit, availability, quality, location, and balance exceptions against refinery requirements and the supply plan, coordinating timely response, and providing reliable current-position information to planning, trading, and logistics.
CM-1-2-6-1-1: Segment the customers and demand points served by the refined-product supply network on supply-economics dimensions — volume, product mix, location, delivery mode, service requirements, and margin contribution — so participation, service, and cost-to-serve analysis work from an economically meaningful segmentation.
CM-1-2-6-1-2: Evaluate market attractiveness for supply-network participation using accessible demand, realizable supply margin, logistics reach and cost, supply reliability, specification and regulatory constraints, and network fit — so participation recommendations rest on a consistent supply-network economic evaluation.
CM-1-2-6-1-3: Assess the full cost of serving customers, segments, and markets from the refined-product supply network — supply, storage, handling, primary and secondary logistics, and service costs against realized margins — identifying where the network serves profitably, marginally, or at a loss, so participation and service recommendations rest on evidenced economics.
